workflow.name: bug-report-triage
workflow.description: 4-step bug triage pipeline: bug classification, severity assessment, root cause hypothesis, and triage recommendation.

cases.label: null-pointer-payment-flow
cases.report: BUG-4471: NullPointerException thrown in PaymentProcessor.charge() when user submits checkout with a saved card that was created before the 2024-03 schema migration. Stack trace: PaymentProcessor.java:187 -> TokenResolver.resolve() -> CardVaultClient.getToken(). Affects ~3% of users with legacy saved cards. Error rate: 0.8% of all checkout attempts. Reproducible 100% on accounts created before 2024-03-15.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Runtime Exception — NullPointerException in payment processing hot path. Type: Regression (introduced by 2024-03 schema migration). Component: PaymentProcessor → TokenResolver → CardVaultClient chain. Scope: 3% of user base (legacy saved card holders). Impact surface: checkout flow — revenue-critical path.
cases.bc_b: NullPointerException in payment flow. Caused by schema migration. Affects some users.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P1 — CRITICAL. Justification: (1) Directly blocks checkout for ~3% of user base on 100% reproducible basis; (2) Revenue impact: 0.8% checkout failure rate — at any meaningful transaction volume this is material daily revenue loss; (3) Payment flow failure has secondary effects: abandoned carts, customer support tickets, potential chargeback disputes; (4) 100% reproducibility makes this not a flaky issue — every affected user hitting checkout will fail. SLA: Resolution within 4 hours, mitigation within 1 hour.
cases.sa_b: Severity: High. Affects payment flow. Revenue impact. Needs urgent fix.
cases.rc_a: Root cause hypothesis: The 2024-03 schema migration likely introduced a new nullable field in the card token schema (e.g., card_vault_id or token_version). CardVaultClient.getToken() returns null for legacy cards that pre-date this field and were not backfilled during migration. TokenResolver.resolve() dereferences the result without a null check, causing NPE at PaymentProcessor.java:187. Secondary hypothesis: The migration may have renamed an existing column without updating the CardVaultClient query, causing the ORM to return null for unmapped fields. Confirm by checking: (1) migration diff for cards table; (2) CardVaultClient.getToken() return type handling; (3) whether legacy cards were backfilled post-migration.
cases.rc_b: Likely the schema migration changed something that legacy cards depend on. CardVaultClient is probably returning null for old cards.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 1h): Add null check in TokenResolver.resolve() — if getToken() returns null, route to legacy token fallback path or throw a handled PaymentException with user-facing 'please re-add your card' message. Deploy as hotfix. SHORT-TERM (< 24h): Audit the 2024-03 migration diff — identify the specific schema change affecting legacy cards. Write a backfill script for all pre-2024-03-15 cards to populate the missing field. Add integration test covering legacy card checkout path to regression suite. LONG-TERM: Add CardVaultClient contract tests to CI pipeline. Implement migration verification step that runs checkout simulation against a sample of legacy accounts before marking a migration complete.
cases.tr_b: Add a null check in TokenResolver. Run a backfill for old cards. Add a test for this case.

cases.label: memory-leak-worker-service
cases.report: BUG-5892: Worker service (document-processor) memory usage climbs from ~200MB at startup to >2GB over 6-8 hours before OOMKilled by Kubernetes. Heap dumps show accumulation of DocumentContext objects that are not being garbage collected. Leak rate correlates with document processing volume. Started appearing after v2.4.1 deploy (3 weeks ago). P99 processing latency also degraded 40% over the same period.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Memory Leak — heap accumulation in document processing worker. Type: Regression introduced in v2.4.1 (3 weeks ago). Component: document-processor worker service — DocumentContext object lifecycle. Pattern: objects accumulating without GC — classic reference retention leak. Secondary effect: 40% P99 latency degradation (GC pressure as heap fills).
cases.bc_b: Memory leak in worker service. DocumentContext objects not being garbage collected. Started after v2.4.1.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — HIGH. Justification: (1) Service OOMKills every 6-8 hours — regular automatic restarts disrupting processing pipeline; (2) 40% P99 latency degradation impacts SLA for document processing customers; (3) Kubernetes restart cycle creates processing gaps — in-flight documents at restart time may be dropped or double-processed depending on at-least-once vs at-most-once semantics; (4) Scales with volume — higher traffic = faster OOMKill cycle. Not P1 because: service restarts automatically (not a hard outage) and the leak rate is predictable. Escalate to P1 if OOMKill cycle drops below 2 hours.
cases.sa_b: Severity: High. Service is restarting regularly. Performance degraded.
cases.rc_a: Root cause hypothesis: v2.4.1 likely introduced a listener, callback, or cache that holds a reference to DocumentContext objects, preventing GC. Most probable candidates: (1) Event listener registration in DocumentContext constructor without corresponding deregister on completion — common Java/Kotlin leak pattern; (2) A new static cache or ConcurrentHashMap added in v2.4.1 that stores DocumentContext references without eviction policy; (3) Thread-local variable storing DocumentContext that is set but never cleared after worker thread completes processing. Confirm by: (1) diffing v2.4.0 → v2.4.1 for any new static fields, caches, or listener registrations in DocumentContext and its dependencies; (2) running VisualVM or async-profiler against a running instance to identify GC roots retaining DocumentContext; (3) checking heap dump for which object holds the surviving DocumentContext references.
cases.rc_b: Something in v2.4.1 is holding references to DocumentContext. Probably a cache or listener that wasn't cleaned up.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 4h): Identify the retaining reference via heap dump GC root analysis — this should take < 30 minutes with a heap dump already available. Once identified: patch the retention point (remove static ref, add cache eviction, clear thread-local). Deploy patch to staging, validate with memory profiling over 1 hour under synthetic load. ROLLBACK OPTION: If patch takes > 4h, consider rolling back to v2.4.0 to stop the bleed while fix is prepared. SHORT-TERM (< 48h): Add memory-based alerting: alert at 1GB (warning) and 1.5GB (critical) with heap dump auto-capture. Add DocumentContext lifecycle test to CI — assert no surviving references after processing completes. LONG-TERM: Introduce static analysis rule (PMD/SpotBugs) flagging unclosed listeners and non-evicting caches. Add weekly heap analysis to performance regression suite.
cases.tr_b: Find what's holding the references in the heap dump. Fix the retention. Roll back to v2.4.0 if needed. Add memory alerting.

cases.label: race-condition-order-status
cases.report: BUG-6103: Intermittent duplicate order confirmation emails sent to customers. Occurs when two concurrent webhook events arrive from payment provider within ~200ms of each other (payment.succeeded + payment.captured). Both events trigger the order fulfilment workflow independently. Rate: ~0.3% of orders. Customer complaints up 12% this month. Worse under high load.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Race Condition — concurrent webhook event processing causing duplicate workflow trigger. Type: Concurrency bug in event-driven order fulfilment pipeline. Trigger: payment.succeeded + payment.captured events arriving within ~200ms window. Pattern: non-idempotent event consumer without deduplication guard. Impact: duplicate fulfilment workflow executions, duplicate customer emails. Load-sensitive: worse under high concurrency.
cases.bc_b: Race condition causing duplicate emails. Two payment webhook events triggering the same workflow.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — HIGH. Justification: (1) Directly impacts customer experience — duplicate order confirmations create confusion, support tickets, and trust erosion; (2) 0.3% order rate — at scale this is significant absolute volume; (3) Risk of duplicate fulfilment actions beyond emails: if the race condition also triggers inventory reservation or shipping label creation twice, financial and operational impact is material; (4) Worse under load — problem self-amplifies during peak traffic. Confirm whether duplicate emails are the only side effect: check for duplicate inventory decrements, shipping label creation, or payment capture attempts.
cases.sa_b: Severity: Medium-High. Customers getting duplicate emails. Needs fixing before it gets worse.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: The order fulfilment workflow consumer is not idempotent — it processes any qualifying payment event without checking whether the workflow has already been triggered for the same order_id. The payment provider sends both payment.succeeded and payment.captured as separate events (standard Stripe/Adyen behaviour), and both match the workflow trigger condition. Under normal latency, one arrives and is processed before the second; under high load or ~200ms concurrent arrival, both are dequeued and processed by separate worker threads simultaneously before either has committed the 'order fulfilled' state. Fix requires idempotency at the consumer level, not rate-limiting at the infrastructure level.
cases.rc_b: The webhook consumer isn't checking if it already processed an event for this order. Both events match the trigger and get processed independently.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 2h): Add an idempotency guard in the fulfilment workflow trigger: before starting the workflow for an order_id, acquire a distributed lock (Redis SETNX with TTL) or use a DB unique constraint on (order_id, workflow_type). If lock not acquired, log and discard — treat as duplicate. This stops new duplicates without requiring payment provider changes. SHORT-TERM (< 1 week): Review all webhook event consumers for the same pattern — any non-idempotent consumer is a latent race condition. Implement an event deduplication table: store processed (event_id, order_id) pairs for 24h; reject duplicates at intake. Add integration test: submit two identical webhook events with 50ms gap, assert single workflow execution. LONG-TERM: Adopt outbox pattern or saga pattern for order state transitions — make workflow triggering transactional and idempotent by design, not by guard.
cases.tr_b: Add a lock or unique constraint before triggering the workflow. Check if other consumers have the same issue. Write a test for concurrent webhook delivery.

cases.label: api-timeout-third-party
cases.report: BUG-7034: User-facing API responses degraded. Root cause traced to upstream dependency: AddressValidation service (third-party, Loqate API) timing out under load. Default timeout 30s. P95 response time for /api/checkout/address endpoint: 28s. User sessions timing out before response. Affects address validation at checkout. Loqate confirmed intermittent latency spikes on their end.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Third-Party Dependency Timeout — upstream Loqate API latency causing user-facing degradation. Type: Resilience gap — synchronous hard dependency on non-SLA'd third-party service in checkout critical path. Impact: /api/checkout/address endpoint P95 28s — user session timeout before response. Scope: all users requiring address validation at checkout (all new addresses). Root issue: tight coupling of checkout critical path to a third-party service with no fallback.
cases.bc_b: Third-party address validation API is slow. Causing timeouts at checkout.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — HIGH (functionally P1 for new address checkout flows). Justification: (1) 28s P95 at checkout = most users experiencing timeout before page responds; (2) Checkout abandonment at this latency is near-certain — industry data shows >3s increases checkout abandonment by 40%+; (3) Hard dependency means Loqate degradation = our degradation, with no decoupling; (4) Loqate has confirmed intermittent spikes — this will recur. Revenue impact: direct correlation with checkout completion rate.
cases.sa_b: High severity. Checkout is effectively broken for many users when Loqate is slow.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: AddressValidation service is synchronously blocking the checkout request thread for up to 30s waiting for Loqate. No timeout override, no circuit breaker, no cached fallback, no graceful degradation path. When Loqate spikes, every concurrent checkout request waits the full 30s. The architectural problem: address validation is in the checkout critical path as a synchronous hard dependency, when it could be: (a) asynchronous (validate post-submission); (b) cached (most addresses repeat); (c) degradable (allow unvalidated addresses through with a warning). The 30s default timeout compounds the issue — should be 2-3s max for a user-facing checkout step.
cases.rc_b: The timeout is set too high (30s) and there's no fallback if Loqate is slow. Address validation is blocking checkout.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 1h): Reduce Loqate timeout from 30s to 3s. If Loqate doesn't respond in 3s, skip validation and allow checkout to proceed — log the skip for async validation. This immediately restores checkout for users during Loqate spikes. SHORT-TERM (< 1 week): Implement circuit breaker (Resilience4j or equivalent) on AddressValidation service: open circuit after 5 consecutive timeouts, return fallback (pass-through) for 60s, then half-open probe. Add address validation result cache (Redis, 7-day TTL) — most users reuse addresses, eliminating the dependency for repeat checkouts. Instrument Loqate call latency as a separate metric with alerting at P95 > 1s. LONG-TERM: Move address validation out of the checkout critical path — validate asynchronously post-order submission, flag invalid addresses for follow-up rather than blocking checkout. Evaluate alternative providers (Google Places API, Postcodes.io) for fallback.
cases.tr_b: Reduce the timeout to 3s and add a fallback to skip validation. Add a circuit breaker. Cache validation results.

cases.label: auth-token-not-invalidated
cases.report: BUG-8210: Security issue — JWT tokens remain valid after user explicitly logs out or changes password. Token expiry is set to 24h. Confirmed: logging out only clears the client-side cookie, does not invalidate the server-side token. An attacker with a stolen token can continue to authenticate for up to 24h post-logout. Discovered during internal security review. No evidence of exploitation yet.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Security Vulnerability — JWT token invalidation failure on logout/password change. Type: Authentication logic flaw — stateless JWT implementation without revocation mechanism. OWASP Category: A07:2021 – Identification and Authentication Failures. Scope: all authenticated users. Risk: stolen tokens remain valid for up to 24h post-logout. Discovery: internal security review (no evidence of exploitation).
cases.bc_b: JWT tokens not invalidated on logout. Security issue. Tokens valid for 24h even after logout.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P1 — CRITICAL (Security). Justification: (1) Failure to invalidate tokens on logout is a foundational authentication vulnerability — OWASP Top 10 A07; (2) Any user whose token is stolen (XSS, network intercept, compromised device) cannot protect themselves by logging out; (3) Password change not invalidating tokens means a compromised account remains accessible to an attacker even after the user resets credentials; (4) 24h window is very long — most session hijacking attacks succeed within minutes of token theft. Treat as a security incident, not a standard bug. Requires immediate fix regardless of exploitation evidence.
cases.sa_b: Critical security bug. Must be fixed urgently. Tokens should not be usable after logout.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: The system uses stateless JWTs without a server-side revocation mechanism. Logout clears the client cookie but the JWT itself remains cryptographically valid until its 24h exp claim expires. The authentication middleware validates only the JWT signature and expiry — it does not check a revocation list. This is a known limitation of stateless JWT: revocation requires either: (a) short expiry (< 15 min) + refresh token rotation; or (b) server-side token blocklist/denylist checked on each request. Neither is implemented. Password change has the same gap — no mechanism to invalidate outstanding tokens issued before the change.
cases.rc_b: JWTs are stateless so logout can't invalidate them server-side. Need a blocklist or shorter expiry.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 4h): Implement a token denylist in Redis: on logout or password change, add the token's jti (JWT ID) claim to a Redis SET with TTL matching the token's remaining expiry. Update authentication middleware to check the denylist on every request (Redis GET is ~1ms — negligible overhead). Deploy and verify logout now invalidates all sessions. SAME DAY: Rotate JWT signing secret — this invalidates all currently active tokens, forcing re-login for all users. Acceptable disruption given the security severity. Communicate to users as 'security update requiring re-login.' SHORT-TERM (< 1 week): Reduce JWT expiry from 24h to 15 minutes. Implement refresh token rotation (opaque, server-side, single-use). Add logout-all-devices endpoint for users who suspect compromise. LONG-TERM: Security review of all authentication and session management flows against OWASP ASVS Level 2 checklist. Add automated security regression tests for auth token lifecycle.
cases.tr_b: Add a Redis denylist for revoked tokens. Check it on every auth request. Also reduce token expiry to 15 minutes and add refresh tokens.

cases.label: sql-injection-search-endpoint
cases.report: BUG-9001: Potential SQL injection vulnerability identified in /api/products/search endpoint. The 'category' query parameter is interpolated directly into a raw SQL query string without parameterisation. Discovered by penetration tester. PoC: category=electronics' OR '1'='1 returns all products regardless of category. No evidence of exploitation in logs.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Security Vulnerability — SQL Injection in product search endpoint. Type: Input validation failure — unsanitised user input interpolated into raw SQL. OWASP Category: A03:2021 – Injection (consistently ranked top 3 web vulnerability). CVE potential: yes, if externally reported. Endpoint: /api/products/search?category=. Discovery: penetration test (professional engagement).
cases.bc_b: SQL injection in search endpoint. Category parameter not sanitised. Pen test finding.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P0 — CRITICAL (Security). Justification: (1) SQL injection is the most dangerous web vulnerability class — OWASP A03:2021; (2) The PoC demonstrates data exfiltration capability (OR 1=1 returns all rows) — in a more sophisticated attack, UNION SELECT could exfiltrate users, passwords, payment data; (3) Depending on DB user permissions, this may allow writes (UPDATE/DELETE) or even command execution (xp_cmdshell on MSSQL, LOAD DATA INFILE on MySQL); (4) This is externally exploitable on a public endpoint; (5) Must be treated as a potential data breach event until exploitation is confirmed absent. Immediate escalation to CISO and legal team required.
cases.sa_b: Critical security issue. SQL injection can expose all data. Fix immediately.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: The developer used raw SQL string interpolation instead of parameterised queries or ORM query builders. Example pattern: `query = 'SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = \'' + category + '\''`. This is a well-understood, 20-year-old vulnerability class that is entirely preventable with parameterised queries. Likely introduced because: (a) no static analysis/SAST tool in CI pipeline flagging raw SQL; (b) no code review checklist item for SQL parameterisation; (c) developer may have been unaware of the vulnerability. Scope check required: audit all other endpoints for the same pattern — if category is vulnerable, other parameters likely are too.
cases.rc_b: Raw SQL string concatenation with user input. Should use parameterised queries. Probably exists in other endpoints too.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 1h): Patch /api/products/search to use parameterised queries (PreparedStatement in Java, $1 placeholders in PostgreSQL, ORM query builder). Do not sanitise/escape as the fix — parameterise. Deploy to production immediately. This is a P0 — skip standard release process, follow emergency security patch procedure. SAME DAY: Run a SAST scan (Semgrep, Checkmarx, or SonarQube with SQL injection rules) across the entire codebase to identify all other instances of raw SQL string concatenation with user input. Each finding is a separate P0. Preserve server logs from the past 90 days — review for any evidence of exploitation (unusual query patterns, error logs indicating malformed SQL from injection attempts). INCIDENT RESPONSE: Brief CISO. If any exploitation evidence found: treat as data breach, engage legal and DPO, follow GDPR Art. 33 72-hour notification timeline. LONG-TERM: Add SAST to CI pipeline — fail build on SQL injection patterns. Implement parameterised query linting rule. Conduct developer security training. Quarterly pen testing schedule.
cases.tr_b: Fix the query to use parameterised statements immediately. Scan the rest of the codebase. Save logs to check for exploitation. Notify security team.

cases.label: ui-rendering-glitch-safari
cases.report: BUG-3344: Dashboard charts fail to render on Safari 17 (macOS Sonoma). White boxes appear where charts should be. Console error: 'ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded'. Affects Safari 17 only — Chrome, Firefox, Edge all fine. Approximately 8% of our users use Safari 17. Charts work on Safari 16.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Browser Compatibility Bug — Safari 17 rendering failure for dashboard charts. Type: Regression introduced by Safari 17 update (not our code change). Root indicator: 'ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded' — known Safari 17 behaviour difference vs Chrome/Firefox. Scope: 8% of user base (Safari 17). Charts affected: all dashboard charts (white box = component mount failure).
cases.bc_b: Safari 17 chart rendering broken. ResizeObserver error. 8% of users affected.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P3 — MEDIUM. Justification: (1) 8% of user base with complete dashboard chart failure is material but not revenue-critical; (2) Dashboard is read-only (no transaction risk); (3) Workaround available (use Chrome); (4) Not our regression — Safari behaviour change. Escalation trigger: if Safari usage > 15% or if charts contain business-critical operational data with no alternative view. Context: Safari 17 changed how it handles ResizeObserver callbacks — it now fires a hard limit error where Chrome silently absorbs the loop.
cases.sa_b: Medium severity. 8% of users affected. Charts are broken but it's a read-only feature.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: The charting library (likely Chart.js, ECharts, or a similar canvas/SVG-based library) uses ResizeObserver to detect container size changes and re-render. Safari 17 introduced stricter enforcement of the ResizeObserver loop limit — when a resize observation triggers a DOM change that triggers another observation in the same frame, Safari 17 throws 'ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded' and aborts. Chrome and Firefox handle this more permissively. The fix is to debounce or batch the resize callback, preventing the loop from occurring within a single frame. This is a known issue with several charting libraries post-Safari 17.
cases.rc_b: Safari 17 is stricter about ResizeObserver loops. The charting library triggers a loop that Safari won't allow.
cases.tr_a: SHORT-TERM (< 3 days): Wrap the ResizeObserver callback in requestAnimationFrame() to batch observations outside the current paint frame — this is the standard fix for this Safari 17 issue. Alternatively, debounce the resize handler with a 16ms (1 frame) delay. Test fix against Safari 17 on both macOS Sonoma and iOS 17 (same engine). If the charting library exposes a ResizeObserver configuration option, check for a debounce setting before patching manually. Check if a newer version of the charting library already includes this fix — upgrade may be cleaner than patching. Add Safari 17 to the browser compatibility test matrix in CI (currently missing — this was caught by user report, not automated test). LONG-TERM: Add Safari to Playwright/Cypress browser matrix for chart rendering smoke tests. Subscribe to Safari WebKit release notes for breaking API changes.
cases.tr_b: Wrap ResizeObserver callback in requestAnimationFrame. Check if the chart library has a fix. Add Safari to browser testing.

cases.label: database-deadlock-high-load
cases.report: BUG-10234: Database deadlocks occurring on the orders table during peak traffic (Black Friday simulation load test). Deadlock rate: 1.2% of concurrent order creation attempts. PostgreSQL logs show deadlock between two transactions: TX1 acquires row lock on orders then inventory, TX2 acquires row lock on inventory then orders. Classic lock ordering inversion. Load test: 500 concurrent order creations. Production order volume: ~120/min peak.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Database Deadlock — lock ordering inversion between order creation transactions. Type: Concurrency bug — inconsistent lock acquisition order between two transaction paths. Tables involved: orders + inventory (bidirectional lock dependency). Pattern: classic AB-BA deadlock. Discovery: load test (Black Friday simulation at 500 concurrent). Production risk: deadlock rate scales with concurrency — at 120/min peak this may not surface, but Black Friday volumes will.
cases.bc_b: Database deadlock between orders and inventory tables. Two transactions acquiring locks in opposite order.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — HIGH (pre-production, but P1-equivalent for Black Friday readiness). Justification: (1) 1.2% deadlock rate at 500 concurrent is significant — PostgreSQL deadlock resolution results in transaction abort and client-side retry burden; (2) If not fixed before Black Friday: at 500+ concurrent orders, this will cause visible checkout failures and require automatic retries adding latency; (3) Deadlocks are deterministic at sufficient concurrency — this will manifest in production at projected peak load; (4) Customer-facing symptom: 'Order failed, please try again' errors during peak. Treat as a pre-production P1 for the Black Friday readiness milestone.
cases.sa_b: High severity. Will cause real problems at Black Friday volumes. Need to fix before peak.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: Two independent transaction paths access the orders and inventory tables but in opposite lock order. TX1 (order creation flow): INSERT orders → UPDATE inventory (locks orders first, then inventory). TX2 (inventory reservation flow): SELECT FOR UPDATE inventory → UPDATE orders status (locks inventory first, then orders). When TX1 and TX2 run concurrently, TX1 holds an orders lock waiting for inventory while TX2 holds an inventory lock waiting for orders — classic ABBA deadlock. Resolution: enforce a consistent lock acquisition order across all transactions touching both tables. Standard approach: always lock in alphabetical table order, or always lock the lower-PK row first, or refactor to avoid needing both locks simultaneously.
cases.rc_b: TX1 locks orders then inventory, TX2 locks inventory then orders. Need to make them consistent.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 1 day): Refactor TX2 (inventory reservation) to acquire the orders lock first, matching TX1's order: SELECT FOR UPDATE orders → UPDATE inventory. This eliminates the ABBA cycle. Validate in the load test environment at 500+ concurrent. The fix is a single transaction reordering — low risk, high impact. SHORT-TERM (< 1 week): Audit all transactions touching orders and inventory for lock ordering consistency — document the canonical lock order and enforce it as a team standard. Add a load test to the CI regression suite: run 200 concurrent order creations and assert 0 deadlocks. Implement PostgreSQL deadlock alert: alert on any deadlock_count > 0 in pg_stat_activity during production. LONG-TERM: Consider optimistic concurrency control for inventory reservation (version column + retry on conflict) — eliminates the need for SELECT FOR UPDATE and removes the lock dependency entirely. This is a more scalable pattern for high-throughput order systems.
cases.tr_b: Make TX2 acquire the orders lock before the inventory lock. Audit other transactions. Add a load test to catch this.

cases.label: payment-processing-error-rate
cases.report: BUG-11450: Payment processing error rate increased from baseline 0.1% to 1.8% over the past 48 hours. Stripe webhook delivery logs show 18% of webhooks arriving with >5s delay. Payment status updates delayed: orders stuck in 'pending' state for up to 10 minutes before resolving. Support ticket volume up 35%. Root cause not yet identified.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Payment Infrastructure Degradation — elevated error rate + Stripe webhook delivery delay. Type: Systemic performance issue (not a single transaction failure). Components: Stripe webhook delivery pipeline + payment status update consumer. Symptom: orders stuck in 'pending' → customer-visible payment uncertainty → support ticket spike. 48h timeline + 18x error rate increase suggests a specific change or external dependency change as trigger.
cases.bc_b: Payment error rate up from 0.1% to 1.8%. Stripe webhooks delayed. Orders stuck as pending.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P1 — CRITICAL. Justification: (1) Payment processing is the primary revenue flow — 1.8% error rate at any meaningful transaction volume is direct revenue leakage; (2) Orders stuck in 'pending' creates customer uncertainty, chargeback risk, and inventory reservation issues; (3) 35% support ticket spike indicates widespread customer impact; (4) 48h duration without resolution suggests the trigger has not been identified; (5) Stripe webhook delay of 18% is abnormally high — Stripe's SLA is typically 99.9% delivery within 1s. Requires immediate war room if not already active.
cases.sa_b: P1. Revenue impacted. Support tickets up. Needs immediate investigation.
cases.rc_a: Investigation priorities in order: (1) Check Stripe's status page (status.stripe.com) — if Stripe is reporting a webhook delivery incident, the root cause is external and the immediate response is different (implement polling fallback, communicate to customers); (2) Check webhook endpoint health: is the /webhooks/stripe endpoint returning 200 reliably? Stripe retries on non-200 — if the endpoint is intermittently failing, Stripe queues retries causing the delay; (3) Check recent deployments in the past 48h — any change to webhook handler, authentication, or infrastructure that correlates with onset; (4) Check webhook consumer queue depth and processing rate — if the consumer is behind (queue depth growing), webhooks arrive but aren't processed promptly; (5) Check database connection pool saturation — payment status update writes competing with other traffic under load.
cases.rc_b: Check Stripe's status page. Check if webhook endpoint is healthy. Look for a recent deployment that might have caused this.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 30 min): Check Stripe status page and Stripe Dashboard → Webhooks → Recent deliveries. If Stripe-side: communicate to customers, enable payment status polling as fallback (query Stripe API directly for payment_intent status every 30s for orders in pending state > 5min). If our-side: identify the failing component from webhook delivery logs and triage accordingly. WITHIN 1H: Enable real-time monitoring on webhook endpoint response codes, consumer queue depth, and payment status update latency. If queue depth is growing: scale up webhook consumer instances. Review all deployments in past 48h — if a specific commit correlates with onset, rollback as the fastest path to resolution. SHORT-TERM: Implement a payment status reconciliation job: every 5 minutes, query Stripe API for all orders in 'pending' state > 3 minutes and force-update their status. This decouples customer order resolution from webhook delivery reliability. LONG-TERM: Implement dual-path payment status resolution: webhooks as primary, polling reconciliation as fallback — standard pattern for payment systems requiring 99.9%+ reliability.
cases.tr_b: Check Stripe status page first. Look for recent deploys. Add a reconciliation job for stuck orders. Scale the webhook consumer if queue is backing up.

cases.label: session-expiry-premature
cases.report: BUG-12001: Users being logged out prematurely — session expires after 15-20 minutes of active use instead of the configured 8-hour session timeout. Affects ~12% of users, seemingly correlated with users on mobile devices or with multiple browser tabs open. No errors in application logs. Session cookie appears to be cleared. Started after infrastructure migration to new load balancer (HAProxy → Nginx) 2 weeks ago.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Session Management Bug — premature session expiry post load balancer migration. Type: Infrastructure regression — likely sticky session or session affinity misconfiguration in Nginx replacing HAProxy. Scope: ~12% of users, mobile/multi-tab correlation. Discovery: user reports (not caught by monitoring — no app-level errors). Trigger: Nginx load balancer migration 2 weeks ago.
cases.bc_b: Users being logged out too early. Happened after load balancer migration. Affects 12% of users.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — HIGH. Justification: (1) 12% of users experiencing unexpected logouts degrades experience significantly — in SaaS, unexpected logouts are one of the highest-friction events and a known churn driver; (2) Mobile users disproportionately affected — often the highest-value user segment in consumer products; (3) 15-20 minute effective session length vs 8-hour configured is a severe discrepancy; (4) No app-level errors makes this invisible to standard monitoring — likely already impacting many more users than have reported. Not P1 because: not a security issue, and users can re-authenticate. Escalate to P1 if session expiry is found to be associated with data loss.
cases.sa_b: High severity. 12% of users randomly logged out. Bad experience especially on mobile.
cases.rc_a: Root cause hypothesis: The Nginx migration almost certainly broke session affinity (sticky sessions). If the application uses server-side sessions (session data stored in memory on application instances, not in a shared store like Redis), requests must be routed to the same application instance that holds the session. HAProxy was configured with sticky sessions (cookie or IP hash); Nginx may not have been configured with the equivalent (ip_hash or sticky cookie). Result: requests from the same user hit different application instances — the instance receiving the request has no record of the session, considers it expired, and clears the cookie. Mobile users and multi-tab users are more likely to hit this because: mobile networks change IP addresses frequently (breaking IP hash affinity), and multiple tabs generate parallel requests that round-robin to different instances. Definitive test: disable all but one application instance — if premature logouts stop, it confirms session affinity is the cause.
cases.rc_b: Nginx probably isn't configured for sticky sessions like HAProxy was. Requests hitting different servers that don't have the session.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 2h): Test hypothesis: check Nginx upstream configuration for ip_hash or sticky cookie directive. If absent, add nginx sticky cookie module configuration to route users to the same upstream based on a session cookie. Alternatively (faster): migrate session storage to Redis — this makes sessions available to all instances regardless of routing, eliminating the need for sticky sessions entirely. Redis session storage is the production-grade solution; sticky sessions are a workaround. Deploy to staging, verify 0 premature logouts under multi-tab and mobile simulation. SHORT-TERM (< 1 week): Migrate session storage to Redis (if not doing it as the immediate fix). This is the correct architectural pattern for load-balanced applications — do not rely on sticky sessions for session state. Add a session health check to the monitoring suite: synthetic user test that logs in, waits 30 min with periodic activity, and alerts if unexpectedly logged out. LONG-TERM: Infrastructure change checklist to include session affinity verification before any load balancer change. Automated canary test on load balancer migrations.
cases.tr_b: Check Nginx for sticky session config. Either add ip_hash or migrate sessions to Redis. Redis is the better long-term fix.

cases.label: data-corruption-csv-export
cases.report: BUG-13302: CSV export feature producing corrupted output when report data contains commas, newlines, or double quotes in text fields. Fields are not quoted or escaped. Example: a company name 'Smith, Jones & Co' exports as three separate columns. Affects all CSV exports. Introduced in v3.1.0 when the CSV generation library was replaced.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Data Integrity Bug — CSV output format violation. Type: Regression introduced in v3.1.0 (library replacement). Root cause category: RFC 4180 CSV compliance failure — text fields containing special characters (comma, newline, double quote) not enclosed in double quotes and not properly escaped. Scope: all CSV exports for any dataset containing text fields with commas/newlines/quotes — likely widespread.
cases.bc_b: CSV export broken when fields contain commas or quotes. Regression from library change in v3.1.0.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — HIGH. Justification: (1) Data integrity issue — exported CSV data is factually wrong (fields split incorrectly), which means any downstream system or user consuming the export is working with corrupted data; (2) Business names, addresses, and description fields commonly contain commas — this likely affects a majority of real-world exports; (3) Silent corruption — the file exports without error, so users may not notice until data analysis is already done on bad data; (4) Affects all CSV exports — not a corner case. Silent data corruption in a reporting feature is higher severity than a visible error.
cases.sa_b: High severity. All CSV exports with commas in fields are wrong. Silent corruption is bad.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: The replacement CSV library in v3.1.0 does not automatically quote fields containing special characters, or the integration code is calling the library's raw write API instead of the properly-escaping API. RFC 4180 requires: (1) fields containing commas, double quotes, or newlines MUST be enclosed in double quotes; (2) double quotes within a quoted field MUST be escaped as two double quotes ('""'). The previous library handled this automatically; the new library either requires explicit configuration or the developer used the wrong method. Fix is straightforward: configure the new library to quote all fields (safer) or implement proper RFC 4180 quoting in the integration layer.
cases.rc_b: New CSV library isn't quoting fields with special characters. Need to configure it correctly or wrap fields manually.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 2h): Identify the new CSV library's quoting API — most libraries have a 'quote all fields' mode or a field-level quote method. Enable it. If the library lacks proper RFC 4180 support, replace it with a compliant one (Apache Commons CSV for Java, Python's built-in csv module, Papa Parse for JS — all handle quoting correctly out of the box). Add a unit test: export a dataset with fields containing commas, double quotes, and newlines — assert the output parses back to the original data without loss. Deploy fix immediately — this is a data integrity issue. SHORT-TERM (< 3 days): Send a notice to users who exported CSVs since v3.1.0 deploy date, advising them to re-export. Provide a list of affected export jobs if available in logs. Add CSV round-trip test to CI: generate → export → import → assert data identity. LONG-TERM: Standardise on a single CSV/data export utility across the codebase. Add RFC 4180 compliance to the library evaluation checklist for any future CSV library changes.
cases.tr_b: Configure the CSV library to quote fields properly or use a different library. Send a notice to affected users. Add a round-trip test.

cases.label: infinite-loop-report-generation
cases.report: BUG-14567: Report generation worker enters an infinite loop when processing reports with circular parent-child category relationships. Worker CPU spikes to 100%, report never completes, worker must be restarted manually. Circular relationships can be created through the category management UI — no validation prevents them. Affects approximately 0.5% of reports. Category tree depth traversal algorithm does not detect cycles.
cases.bc_a: Classification: Infinite Loop — cycle detection absent in category tree traversal algorithm. Type: Algorithm bug — depth-first traversal without visited set, enabling infinite recursion/iteration on circular graphs. Root cause: no validation at data entry (circular relationships creatable via UI) + no cycle detection at traversal time. Impact: worker hang at 100% CPU, manual restart required, 0.5% of reports affected.
cases.bc_b: Infinite loop in report generator when categories have circular relationships. No cycle detection.
cases.sa_a: Severity: P2 — MEDIUM-HIGH. Justification: (1) Worker hang requires manual restart — operational overhead and monitoring gap; (2) 0.5% of reports affected — at scale this is meaningful absolute volume; (3) 100% CPU spike may affect other reports running on the same worker instance (noisy neighbour); (4) The underlying data integrity issue (circular category relationships allowable) is a separate problem that needs addressing at the source. Not P1 because: affects 0.5% of reports, manual workaround exists (restart worker), not a security or revenue-critical path.
cases.sa_b: Medium-High. Worker hangs and needs manual restart. 0.5% of reports affected.
cases.rc_a: Root cause: The category tree traversal algorithm uses a naive depth-first search without maintaining a visited set. For a DAG (directed acyclic graph), this works correctly. For a graph with cycles, traversal revisits nodes indefinitely: A → B → C → A → B → C → ... The algorithm has no termination condition other than reaching leaf nodes (which never happens in a cycle). Two separate problems: (1) Algorithmic: traversal needs a visited set (or path set for proper cycle reporting); (2) Data integrity: the UI allows creation of circular parent-child relationships with no validation — this should be prevented at write time, not caught at read time.
cases.rc_b: Traversal algorithm has no visited set so it loops forever on cycles. Also need to prevent circular relationships from being created.
cases.tr_a: IMMEDIATE (< 4h): Add cycle detection to the traversal algorithm — maintain a visited set; if the current node is already in visited, it's a cycle: throw a CycleDetectedException and fail the report with a clear error message rather than looping. This stops the infinite loop and allows the worker to recover without manual restart. Also add a traversal depth limit (e.g., 1000 nodes) as a safety backstop against other pathological inputs. SHORT-TERM (< 1 week): Add validation at category creation/update: before saving a parent-child relationship, run cycle detection on the proposed graph. Reject the operation if it would create a cycle. Add UI error message: 'This relationship would create a circular dependency.' Write a data migration: identify and report all existing circular relationships in the database for manual remediation. LONG-TERM: Add category graph integrity to the test suite — generate graphs with cycles and assert they are rejected at both write and traversal time. Consider migrating category storage to a graph database or adjacency list model with DB-level constraint enforcement.
cases.tr_b: Add a visited set to the traversal to detect cycles. Add validation in the UI to prevent circular relationships from being created.
